about.title: Hero Grid Tool
about.whatIs.p1: **Hero Grid Tool** is an "alt-tab" tool for building and customizing Dota 2 hero layouts — a personal notebook where you arrange heroes and items into whatever categories make sense to you.
about.whatIs.p2: Use the [Edit](/edit) tab to build a grid: add categories, fill them with heroes and items from the adding dialog or by dragging portraits around, then rename, recolour and resize them. The [View](/view) tab is the clean read-only version you keep next to the game, and [Grids](/layouts) holds every grid you have saved.
about.whatIs.p3: Everything lives in your browser's local storage — nothing is uploaded. Grids travel as self-contained codes, files, links or images.
about.building.categories: **Categories** hold heroes, items, empty slots and row breaks. Each one can override the grid's portrait style, size and item icons.
about.building.chains: **Chains** keep categories together: link them horizontally (adjacent columns) or vertically (stacked rows) with the ↔ and ↕ buttons. A category can be in both.
about.building.breaks: **Row breaks** split a category's portraits onto a new line.
about.building.labels: **Labels** can be free text, one of the presets (lanes, positions, roles, tiers) or a hero/item/facet icon — optionally with a colour tag.
about.building.columns: The column count adapts to the window: a narrow screen caps the number of columns so categories stay readable.
about.autogrid.intro: The **Autogrid** tab in the sidebar builds tier lists straight from the spectral.gg LRG2 stats reports — the same numbers behind [stats.spectral.gg](https://stats.spectral.gg). Pick a report (or type your own report tag), tick the grids you want, and each one is saved under a dated name.
about.autogrid.tiers: **Tiers** — taken from the report's own tier lists where it has them, which are filtered and weighted by meta-level membership on the server. Reports without them fall back to ranking the positions table here: heroes picked less than 90% as often as the median for that position are dropped, and the rest are ordered by their `rank` score and split into six tiers taking 8 / 14 / 20 / 22 / 18 / 18% of the pool. Every grid's description says which of the two it used and lists the rank window each tier covers.
about.autogrid.roleGrids: **Role grids** — one tier per row, coloured by tier.
about.autogrid.total: **Total meta** — a column per role, a tier per row, each column chained vertically and coloured by role, with the strongest heroes overall and the most-banned ones above it and the heroes to avoid this patch underneath.
about.autogrid.overall: **Overall tier list** — the same six tiers with no role split, one row each.
about.autogrid.metaLevels: **Meta levels** — the report's meta layers, oldest first: each row is the heroes that define a layer beside the combo pieces that go with them, followed by any layers the report projects.
about.autogrid.personalIntro: Give it a Steam account id (the Dota friend id) with a public match history and it builds a grid around how *you* play: the report's tiers are re-scored by your record on each hero. Three things move a hero — how you do on it, measured against your own overall win rate rather than 50%; how much you play it, since a hero with hundreds of games behind it is one you can actually pilot, though only while the record holds up; and how little you play it, which drags a hero down unless the report already rates it near the top. All of it is damped by games played, so a couple of lucky games move nothing.
about.autogrid.best: **Best heroes** — the ones you are known for: enough games to mean something and a win rate that stands out from the rest of your pool. If nothing stands out you get a top few instead.
about.autogrid.practice: **Practice** — strong heroes you have hardly played. If you have played everything, it relaxes to the strong heroes you play least.
about.autogrid.bans: **Bans** — the heroes with the best record against you.
about.autogrid.roles: **Roles** — one block each, best-for-you first, optionally ordered by how much you play them (judged by your games on each role's heroes).
about.autogrid.notYet: Rank-bracket selection and meta tier lists are not wired up yet.
about.keys.intro: Every shortcut is **Alt** plus one key, and none of them fire while you are typing in a field.
about.formats.intro: The tool reads every format below — paste it into [Grids → Import](/layouts), drop in a file, or scan a QR code. Imports are detected automatically, so you never have to say which kind it is.
about.formats.codeP: A single grid is packed into a binary record, deflated, and written as URL-safe base64 — typically around a hundred characters, and a fraction of that for large grids. Compression is only kept when it actually makes the code shorter, and codes made before it was introduced still decode. This is what share links carry (`/import?b=<code>`), what **Copy code** puts on your clipboard, and what the `.txt` export contains. The record is, in order:
about.formats.f1: `version` — one byte; older codes still import.
about.formats.f2: `flags` — one byte of board toggles: colourful labels, centered, darkened background, freeform canvas, transparent categories.
about.formats.f4: `name`, `icon`, `author`, `description` — length-prefixed UTF-8 strings (author and description may be empty).
about.formats.f5: `categories` — a count, then one record per category: flags, label (preset id or text), optional icon, colour, width, header size, chain ids, per-category style overrides, and finally its elements.
about.formats.f6: `elements` — one byte of kind and flags each, plus a hero/item id, a custom tag, or nothing for empty slots and row breaks.
about.formats.codeNote: Because the format is positional and versioned, a code always decodes to exactly the grid it came from, and new fields can be added without breaking old links.
about.formats.allP: Your whole collection can be exported at once. That is the JSON list below, deflated and base64 encoded, as used by **Share all** and `/layouts?l=<code>`. Compression matters most here — a few grids shrink by well over 90%.
about.formats.jsonP: The `.json` export is human-readable and diff-friendly — a saved grid, or a list of them:
about.formats.jsonNote: A bare `board` object works too. Hero and item `refId`s are the standard Dota ids, `preset` replaces `text` for preset labels, and `hGroup` / `vGroup` mark chained categories.
about.formats.gameP: The game's own `hero_grid_config.json` is read and written as-is, including a single config object or a fragment cut out of the `configs` array. In-game grids are freeform, so they import as canvas grids; category icons travel as `{S:<tag>}` in the name and a `------` category splits one block into two.
about.formats.oldP: JSON exported from the previous (AngularJS) version of the tool is accepted as-is and converted on import: preset labels, colour tags, widths, the "bigger portraits" flag and hero lists all carry over. Grids left in that version's local storage are converted automatically the first time you open this one. Since old grids had no item or portrait-style settings, converted grids start from the current defaults.
about.sharing.link: **Link** — the grid code in a URL, plus a QR code for getting it onto a phone.
about.sharing.image: **Image** — a PNG of the whole grid, 1600px wide, with the grid name, author, description and a QR code linking back to the editable version.
about.sharing.print: **Print** — Ctrl+P lays the grid out on one page, on white, with the same banner as the image.
about.sharing.files: **Files** — `.txt` for a code, `.json` for one grid or all of them.
about.credits.inspired: Inspired by [this reddit post](https://www.reddit.com/r/DotA2/comments/7iurzb/i_started_creating_a_drafting_chart_around_my/). Hero and item data comes from the spectral.gg LRG2 API; images from the spectral courier CDN.
